practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1933 editorial in a Republican-leaning newspaper attacking the alphabet agencies as wasteful federal overreach) and Interpretation B (a 1934 article by a Tennessee Valley farmer praising the TVA for bringing electricity and flood control). What is the main difference between these views about the First New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the alphabet agencies as a wasteful expansion of federal power that bypassed Congress and undermined private enterprise.
• Interpretation B presents the TVA as a transformation that brought tangible improvements — electricity, flood control, jobs — to one of the poorest regions in America.
• Main difference: A frames the New Deal as overreach by Washington; B frames it as targeted help that local communities welcomed.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1933 Republican editorial) and Interpretation B (a 1934 article by a Tennessee Valley farmer) give different views about the First New Deal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the editorial spoke to readers worried about federal power and big government; the farmer’s article spoke to neighbours who had benefited directly from TVA dams.
• They use different evidence — the editorial cites federal spending and constitutional concerns; the farmer cites electricity reaching his farm and flood damage prevented.
• They were produced from different positions — an urban Republican commentator opposed to Roosevelt versus a rural beneficiary in a poor region transformed by the TVA.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Roosevelt’s first hundred days saved American capitalism from collapse.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the impact of the First New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Emergency Banking Act of 9 March 1933 stopped a banking collapse: $1 billion of deposits flooded back within a fortnight after the four-day bank holiday and Treasury inspections.
• Convincing because Glass-Steagall and the FDIC restored confidence that personal savings up to $5,000 were safe.
• Convincing because the alphabet agencies (CCC, FERA, AAA, NRA, PWA, TVA) employed millions and lifted farm income by around 50% in two years.
• Less convincing because unemployment remained high — around 11 million still out of work in 1934 — and full recovery only came with war production from 1941.
• Less convincing because the Supreme Court later struck down the NRA (1935) and AAA (1936) as unconstitutional, exposing structural weaknesses.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing in stopping the collapse and rebuilding confidence; less convincing as an explanation of full economic recovery.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Emergency Banking Act of March 1933 on the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stopped the banking panic — the four-day bank holiday closed every bank for inspection; only those judged solvent reopened on 13 March, and around $1 billion of cash flooded back into deposits within a fortnight.
• Restored confidence through Roosevelt’s first fireside chat on 12 March, which explained the rescue in plain language to 60 million radio homes — reframing the federal government as protector rather than spectator.
• Created the foundation for further reform — the June 1933 Glass-Steagall Act built on the success by establishing the FDIC, which insured deposits up to $5,000 and separated commercial from investment banking.
• Saved roughly 5,000 sound banks by allowing supervised reopening, and permanently reduced the rate of bank failures — the lifeblood without which alphabet-agency spending could not have circulated through the economy.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Roosevelt’s First New Deal had a major impact on the United States in 1933–34.
You may consider:
• the banking and farm rescue measures
• the alphabet agencies and federal employment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Banking rescue: the Emergency Banking Act (9 March 1933) closed banks for inspection; reopening triggered $1 billion of redeposits; Glass-Steagall (June 1933) created the FDIC insuring savings up to $5,000.
• Farm rescue: the AAA (May 1933) paid farmers to cut production; six million pigs slaughtered; farm income rose around 50% within two years.
• Mass relief: FERA distributed $500 million through Harry Hopkins; CCC employed 2.5 million young men by 1942 at $30/month; CCC built 800 state parks and planted three billion trees.
• Industrial recovery: NRA codes on wages, hours and prices; blue eagle symbol; 2.5 million employers signed up. PWA $3.3 billion built the Hoover Dam, Lincoln Tunnel, Triborough Bridge.
• Regional reform: TVA built 20 dams in seven southern states, brought electricity to over half the valley by 1940 and controlled flooding.
• Communication: fireside chats turned the presidency into a daily presence in 60 million radio homes.
• Limits: 11 million still unemployed in 1934; the New Deal cushioned but did not end the Depression; the Supreme Court later struck down NRA (1935) and AAA (1936).
• Conclusion: the First New Deal’s major impact was political and psychological as well as economic — it stopped the collapse, rebuilt confidence and redrew the role of the federal government in American life, even though full recovery would have to wait for the war.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The CCC enrolled young unmarried men aged 18–25 in conservation work in national forests, parks and on flood-control schemes. Around 2.5 million young men passed through it by 1942.
• Recruits were paid $30 a month, of which $25 was sent home to their families — combining direct relief for young men with cash transfers to households still suffering from unemployment.
• The CCC planted roughly three billion trees, built 800 state parks and constructed thousands of miles of trails — visible improvements to the American landscape that built support for the New Deal.
• It was administered jointly by the Departments of Labor, Interior and Agriculture and the Army, which ran the camps in military style — controversial to some but giving recruits structure and skills.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

Pick two or three effects (banking confidence, farm income, mass relief employment, federal scope) and develop each with a specific example and figure. Examiner reports flag students who write ‘agency soup’ — long lists of initials with no causal link. For 12-mark Period Essays, the misconception to avoid is that the New Deal ended the Depression. The First New Deal cushioned suffering and rebuilt confidence; only the war economy from 1941 returned the USA to full employment.

lessons.title: Effectiveness, Opposition and the Second New Deal

before.content_html:
A New Deal — for Whom?

By 1934 the First New Deal had stopped the collapse, but the Depression had not ended. Around 11 million Americans were still unemployed. As Roosevelt’s programmes settled into operation, the question shifted from ‘will it work?’ to ‘who is it working for?’. The honest answer is uneven: the New Deal helped some groups powerfully and largely failed others. It also drew loud opposition from three different directions — the Supreme Court, congressional Republicans, and radical critics who argued Roosevelt had not gone nearly far enough. The political pressure forced the ‘Second New Deal’ of 1935.

Key Fact

The New Deal helped industrial workers, farmers and the elderly — through union recognition, AAA payments and Social Security pensions. It largely failed African-Americans, Mexican-Americans and Native Americans. Inequality remained a defining feature of recovery.

Who Benefited Most

Industrial workers were among the biggest winners. The 1935 Wagner Act guaranteed the right to join a trade union and bargain collectively. Union membership doubled from around 3.6 million in 1935 to 8.7 million by 1940. Farmers saw their incomes rise by around 50% in two years thanks to AAA payments. Older Americans gained Social Security pensions. Around 8.5 million workers found employment through the Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935) building schools, post offices and roads. White women benefited from FERA and WPA jobs, even where pay was lower than men’s. Eleanor Roosevelt actively lobbied her husband to direct New Deal money towards women, miners and the rural poor.

Who Was Left Out

African-Americans gained much less. The AAA paid landowners to take fields out of production, but the cuts hit black sharecroppers and tenant farmers hardest — many were evicted. NRA codes set lower wages for southern workers, where most black Americans lived. Roosevelt refused to back a federal anti-lynching bill because he needed southern Democratic votes in Congress for the rest of his programme. CCC camps were segregated. Some 200,000 black Americans did join the CCC, and Roosevelt’s informal ‘Black Cabinet’ of African-American advisers (including Mary McLeod Bethune) gave the New Deal a moral language on race that earlier presidents had refused. But on the ground, the colour line held.

Mexican-Americans were excluded from many programmes and roughly 500,000 were ‘repatriated’ — in many cases deported — during the 1930s. Native Americans gained more under the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act, which ended the policy of forced assimilation and restored some tribal land rights, but rural poverty persisted. Domestic and agricultural workers (the bulk of black and Hispanic women’s employment) were excluded from Social Security entirely.

Women’s gains were real but limited. Frances Perkins became the first female Cabinet member as Secretary of Labor. Eleanor Roosevelt held weekly press conferences open only to women reporters and lobbied for women’s relief. Around 8,500 women were enrolled in a women’s version of the CCC. But NRA codes often set female wages below men’s, the CCC excluded married women, and the breadwinner ideology was reinforced rather than challenged. The Depression pushed many married women out of paid work to free up jobs for unemployed men.

Opposition from the Supreme Court

The most damaging early opposition came from the Supreme Court. In Schechter v. United States (May 1935) the Court unanimously struck down the NRA as an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power and federal interference with intra-state commerce. In United States v. Butler (January 1936) the Court struck down the AAA on similar grounds. Roosevelt was furious. In 1937 he proposed his ‘court-packing plan’: legislation that would let him appoint up to six new justices to outvote the conservative bloc. Even Democrats called it dictatorial. Congress rejected the plan, but the Court began to uphold New Deal legislation more sympathetically (the so-called ‘switch in time that saved nine’).

Republican and Radical Opposition

Republicans attacked the New Deal as an attack on individual liberty and a step towards socialism. Critics like Wendell Willkie warned that federal spending was unsustainable and that programmes like the TVA undermined private utility companies. The 1936 Republican candidate Alf Landon was crushed in a landslide — Roosevelt won 46 of 48 states — but Republican opposition would harden through Roosevelt’s second term.

More dangerous, politically, were radical critics who argued that the New Deal had not gone far enough. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana proposed his ‘Share Our Wealth’ programme — confiscate the great fortunes and give every family $5,000 and a guaranteed income. Father Charles Coughlin used his weekly radio broadcasts (40 million listeners at peak) to demand bank nationalisation and silver-backed currency, sliding into open antisemitism by 1936. Dr Francis Townsend proposed a $200-a-month pension for everyone over 60 to be spent within 30 days. Long was assassinated in September 1935; Coughlin was eventually silenced by the Catholic hierarchy. But by 1935 the three radical critics had together convinced Roosevelt that he needed bolder reforms or risked losing the centre to a populist challenger.

Even at the worst of the Depression, around 60 million Americans went to the cinema each week. Hollywood produced screwball comedies and gangster films offering escape; Walt Disney’s Snow White (1937) was the highest-grossing film of the decade. Radio reached 28 million households by 1939; Roosevelt’s fireside chats and Coughlin’s broadcasts both depended on the medium. Federal Project Number One under the WPA paid 40,000 unemployed artists, writers, photographers and musicians — producing post office murals, the Federal Theatre Project and Dorothea Lange’s photographs of migrant workers. Popular culture both distracted from suffering and documented it.

The Second New Deal, 1935

The political pressure produced a sharper, more redistributive package in 1935. The Wagner Act guaranteed union rights, partly answering radical demands for worker power. The Social Security Act of August 1935 created federal pensions for the elderly, unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children — the first national welfare system in American history, though limited (it excluded domestic and agricultural workers). The WPA gave employment to 8.5 million workers between 1935 and 1943. A ‘wealth tax’ raised top federal income tax rates to 75% on the highest earners. Roosevelt’s contribution as president now included not just the Hundred Days but a sustained ability to move with political pressure rather than be broken by it.

Key Fact

The Second New Deal of 1935 included the Wagner Act (union rights), the Social Security Act (pensions, unemployment insurance, aid to dependent children) and the WPA (work for 8.5 million). It was driven by Court strikes, radical pressure and the 1936 election — and was more redistributive than the First New Deal.
before.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Evaluate questions on New Deal effectiveness, the strongest answers handle the ‘helped some, failed others’ tension explicitly — do not write the New Deal off as a failure, but do not pretend it ended inequality either. Examiner reports flag the misconception that the New Deal ended the Depression: it did not, but that does not make it a failure. For 12-mark Period Essays comparing Roosevelt’s contribution against structural factors, weigh his political skill (fireside chats, the 1936 landslide) against the Court rulings, the radicals and the eventual war economy.

lessons.title: The Second World War and American Recovery

before.content_html:
The War That Ended the Depression

In 1940 around 8 million Americans were still out of work and the Depression was in its eleventh year. By 1944 unemployment had effectively disappeared and the United States was producing roughly half of all the world’s manufactured goods. The Second World War achieved what the New Deal could not. Federal spending rose from $9 billion in 1939 to $98 billion by 1944. Forty-million Americans were drawn into uniform or war work between 1941 and 1945. The conflict also reshaped American society at home: black families moved north and west by the million, women entered industries previously closed to them, and the federal government became a permanent presence in everyday life.

Key Fact

Around 8 million Americans were still unemployed in 1940. The war economy from 1941 returned the USA to full employment by 1944. The Second World War — not the New Deal — ended the Great Depression.

Lend Lease and the Path to War

The Neutrality Acts of 1935–37 had committed the USA to staying out of European wars. But by 1940 Britain stood alone against Nazi Germany and could no longer pay cash for American supplies. Roosevelt persuaded Congress to pass the Lend-Lease Act in March 1941, allowing the USA to ‘lend or lease’ weapons, food and oil to Britain and later to the Soviet Union without immediate payment. By 1945 around $50 billion of supplies had been shipped — about $32 billion to Britain, $11 billion to the USSR. Roosevelt described the policy as lending a neighbour your hose if their house was on fire. American factories began to fill with orders even before Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 ended the debate over neutrality. Within four days the United States was at war with Japan, Germany and Italy. The transformation of the American economy — long under way thanks to Lend Lease — now accelerated dramatically.

The Arsenal of Democracy

War production figures dwarf anything the New Deal had attempted. Between 1941 and 1945 the United States built around 297,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks, 8,800 warships and 41 billion rounds of small-arms ammunition. The Ford Willow Run plant in Michigan rolled out a B-24 bomber every 63 minutes at peak. Henry Kaiser’s shipyards launched a Liberty cargo ship in just 4–5 days using assembly-line techniques borrowed from car manufacturing. Roosevelt called the United States ‘the arsenal of democracy’ in a December 1940 fireside chat — by 1945 the description was understatement.

Federal spending pumped this expansion. The War Production Board (1942) directed materials and labour. Wages rose by around 65% during the war as factories competed for workers. Personal income tax was extended to most workers for the first time, and the federal government employed around 4 million people directly. New industries grew up where they had barely existed before — aircraft in Los Angeles and Seattle, shipyards on the Gulf coast, atomic research at Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

The New Deal had spent around $4 billion a year at peak. War spending reached $98 billion in 1944 alone — roughly twenty times larger. Critics of the New Deal argue this proves Keynesian deficit spending works when it is big enough. Defenders of the New Deal point out that wartime spending also conscripted 12 million men into the armed forces (removing them from the unemployment count) and silenced the Supreme Court and Republican opposition that had hobbled the New Deal in peacetime. Both sides agree that without Pearl Harbor it is unclear when the Depression would have ended.

African-Americans and the Double V Campaign

War production opened doors that had been closed. The Pittsburgh Courier launched the Double V Campaign in 1942: victory against fascism abroad, victory against racism at home. A. Philip Randolph, leader of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened a march on Washington in 1941 unless Roosevelt acted. Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 in June 1941 banning discrimination in defence industries and creating the Fair Employment Practices Committee — the first federal civil-rights action since Reconstruction.

During the war around 1.5 million African-Americans moved from the South to northern and western cities for war work — the second wave of the Great Migration. Around a million black Americans served in segregated military units. The Tuskegee Airmen, the all-black 332nd Fighter Group, flew over 15,000 missions and earned a battle reputation that contradicted segregationist arguments about black military performance. Yet violence persisted on the home front: the Detroit race riot of June 1943 left 34 people dead, mostly black.

Women on the Home Front

Women filled the gap left by 12 million servicemen. Around 6 million women joined the workforce between 1941 and 1944, many in heavy industry. Rosie the Riveter — the female industrial worker — became a national symbol after a 1943 Norman Rockwell magazine cover and J. Howard Miller’s ‘We Can Do It’ poster. Women welded ships, riveted aircraft and assembled tanks. Around 350,000 women joined the armed forces in non-combat roles such as the WACs (Women’s Army Corps) and WAVES (Navy). Many earned higher wages than they had ever earned before.

The wartime labour gains for women were partial and contested. Female wages in heavy industry were on average around 60% of men’s. Women were widely expected to give back their jobs at the end of the war. Working mothers struggled with limited childcare, although the 1942 Lanham Act funded around 3,000 federal day-care centres. After 1945 around 4 million women were dismissed from war industries to make way for returning servicemen. But the experience of millions of women earning their own wages in skilled industrial work changed expectations that would resurface in the 1960s.

Around 120,000 Japanese-Americans, two-thirds of them US citizens, were forcibly relocated to internment camps under Executive Order 9066 (February 1942) on the grounds of unproven security risk — one of the worst civil-rights violations of the war. Mexican-American workers came north under the 1942 Bracero Programme to fill agricultural labour shortages. Native Americans served in the armed forces in proportionally higher numbers than any other ethnic group; Navajo ‘Code Talkers’ transmitted unbreakable battlefield codes. Rationing of petrol, sugar, butter, meat and clothing reached every household. Around 17 million victory gardens supplied roughly 40% of the nation’s vegetables by 1944.

A Different America in 1945

By the time Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August, the United States had been transformed. National income had roughly doubled. The federal government, which had taken in $7 billion in 1940, took in $50 billion in 1945. The USA emerged as the world’s leading industrial and military power, the only major combatant whose territory had not been bombed. Roosevelt himself died in office on 12 April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe. His successor, Harry Truman, would inherit an economy and a political settlement reshaped by the war and the demands of the millions of Americans who had served, worked or fought in it.

Key Fact

Federal spending rose from $9 billion (1939) to $98 billion (1944) — about twenty times the New Deal’s peak. Conscription removed 12 million men from the unemployment count. The combination of vast deficit spending and the war economy ended the Depression.

lessons.title: Post-war Prosperity, Consumerism and the American Dream

before.content_html:
From Wartime Workshop to Consumer Society

In 1945 the United States emerged from war as the only major combatant economy that had not been bombed. American factories had built the weapons of victory; in 1946 they began turning out cars, washing machines, televisions and houses for a population that had been waiting through fifteen years of depression and wartime rationing. By 1960, US gross national product had roughly doubled in real terms compared with 1945, and Americans — about 6% of the world’s population — consumed roughly a third of its goods and services. Sociologists called this the ‘American Dream’. Whose dream it actually was — and who paid for it — defines the politics of the next twenty years.

Key Fact

By 1960 US GNP had roughly doubled compared with 1945. Americans were 6% of the world population but consumed around a third of all goods and services. The post-war boom rested on cheap oil, mass car ownership, federal housing finance and the spending power of the GI Bill.

The GI Bill and the Suburbs

The cornerstone of post-war prosperity for white American families was the GI Bill — the 1944 Servicemen’s Readjustment Act. It gave returning veterans low-interest home loans with no down payment, federal money to attend college or vocational training, and a year of unemployment pay. Around 7.8 million veterans took up educational benefits and around 4.3 million bought homes with GI loans. The federal government effectively underwrote the creation of a mass middle class.

Suburbs grew faster than any other kind of community. William Levitt mass-produced houses on a Long Island potato field in 1947 using assembly-line construction. A Levittown three-bedroom house went up in around 16 minutes of labour and sold for $7,990 with no down payment for veterans — about half the cost of a comparable urban apartment. By 1951 Levittown had over 17,000 houses and 70,000 residents. Imitators built suburbs across the country. Between 1948 and 1958 around 13 million new homes were built; by 1960 around a third of all Americans lived in suburbs.

William Levitt’s sales contracts originally banned sale or rental to anyone ‘other than members of the Caucasian race’. The Federal Housing Administration, which underwrote the mortgages, drew ‘redlines’ around mixed-race neighbourhoods and refused to insure loans inside them. The result was that the federal subsidies that built suburban affluence were systematically denied to black families. While Levittown housed 70,000 white residents in 1953, not one was African-American. The post-war boom was racially structured from the foundations up — a fact that would shape the geography of American inequality for decades.

Cars, Highways and the Consumer Boom

Suburbs only worked because of cars. Car registrations rose from around 26 million in 1945 to around 60 million by 1960. Petrol cost roughly 25 cents a gallon. The Interstate Highways Act of 1956, signed by President Eisenhower, committed federal money to build 41,000 miles of motorway connecting major cities — partly justified as a Cold War civil-defence measure. Drive-in cinemas, drive-in restaurants and shopping malls (the first regional shopping mall opened at Northgate, Seattle, in 1950) followed the new highways out of the cities.

Consumer credit fuelled the boom. The Diners Club credit card (1950) and BankAmericard (later Visa, 1958) made it easy to buy now and pay later. Hire-purchase schemes spread to washing machines, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners and televisions. By 1960 around 90% of American households had a television. Advertising spending roughly tripled between 1945 and 1960. Consumer goods became the visible measure of success in a society that no longer had a depression to remember and no major war to fight.

Television, Rock and Roll and Teenage Culture

Television became the cultural common ground. By 1960 the average American household watched around five hours a day. Family sitcoms (Leave It to Beaver, Father Knows Best) projected an image of suburban prosperity built around stay-at-home mothers and breadwinner fathers. Westerns and quiz shows dominated prime time. The 1955 Disneyland park in California was a physical version of the same television world — a clean, controlled fantasy of American prosperity.

For young people, the boom produced the modern teenager. Around 13 million Americans were aged 13–19 by 1956, with disposable incomes their parents had never known. The fusion of black rhythm and blues with white country music produced rock and roll: Bill Haley and his Comets’ ‘Rock Around the Clock’ (1954), Elvis Presley’s ‘Heartbreak Hotel’ (1956), Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Buddy Holly. Television shows like American Bandstand brought rock and roll into living rooms. Cinema followed: James Dean in Rebel Without a Cause (1955) and Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953) gave a face to teenage rebellion. Many parents called this the corruption of American youth; teenagers called it freedom.

The 1950s boom was uneven. Around 22% of Americans still lived in poverty in 1960, including most rural African-Americans, Mexican-Americans, Native Americans on reservations, and elderly Americans without Social Security from agricultural or domestic work. Inner-city neighbourhoods, drained of resources by suburban flight, decayed. Female employment rose to around 19 million by 1960 but largely in low-paid clerical and service work; the breadwinner ideal pushed against women combining careers with motherhood. Critics like John Kenneth Galbraith (The Affluent Society, 1958) and Michael Harrington (The Other America, 1962) argued that the dream had ignored a third of the country — a critique that shaped the policies of the next decade.

A Postcard Society

Post-war America presented itself in postcards: the lawn, the station wagon, the kitchen full of new appliances, the children at a newly built suburban school. Most of those postcards were honest about the families they pictured. They were not honest about the families they did not picture — black families in segregated neighbourhoods, Mexican-American farm labourers, elderly Americans on inadequate pensions, urban poor, dissenting students. The American Dream had genuinely lifted tens of millions into the middle class. It had also defined ‘American’ in narrow terms that would generate the political movements of the 1960s. The 1950s prosperity is the launchpad for civil rights, feminism, and the Great Society.

Key Fact

Levittown houses sold for $7,990 with no down payment for veterans. By 1960 around a third of Americans lived in suburbs and 90% of homes had a TV. But around 22% lived in poverty, redlining excluded black families from suburbs, and women were pushed back into domestic roles after wartime work.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Compare Interpretations question, contrasting interpretations of post-war America are common. Examiners reward students who can show the ‘opportunity for whom, inequality for whom?’ tension — not just an optimistic and pessimistic clash. For 12-mark Period Essays on the strengths and limits of the American Dream, mention the GI Bill and Levittown numbers but always link to who was excluded by redlining and FHA practice. The misconception to avoid: the suburbs were not a neutral product of free choice, they were federally underwritten and racially structured.

lessons.title: McCarthyism and the Red Scare of the 1950s

before.content_html:
A Country in Fear

In 1945 the United States was the only nuclear power. By 1949 the Soviet Union had its own atomic bomb, China had become Communist, and confidential American documents were appearing in Soviet archives. In June 1950 Communist North Korea invaded the South. To many ordinary Americans, the Cold War looked as if it were being lost from the inside — betrayed by spies, intellectuals and Hollywood writers. The result was the second great Red Scare, which dominated American politics from 1947 to 1954. Its central figure was a Republican senator from Wisconsin, Joseph McCarthy, but the machinery of fear was much wider than one man.

Key Fact

Four events triggered the second Red Scare: the Soviet atomic bomb (August 1949), the Communist victory in China (October 1949), the conviction of Alger Hiss (January 1950), and the outbreak of the Korean War (June 1950). These convinced many Americans the country was losing the Cold War from the inside.

HUAC and the Hollywood Ten

The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), originally founded in 1938, became a major political force in October 1947 when it began investigating alleged Communist influence in Hollywood. HUAC summoned 41 writers, directors and actors. Most cooperated; ten refused on First Amendment grounds to answer the question ‘are you now or have you ever been a member of the Communist Party?’. The Hollywood Ten were jailed for contempt of Congress for between six and twelve months.

Hollywood studios, terrified of losing audiences, responded with the ‘Waldorf Statement’ in November 1947 announcing they would not employ Communists. Around 320 entertainment-industry workers were eventually blacklisted; many never worked under their own names again. Charlie Chaplin lost his US re-entry permit in 1952 and never returned. Composer Hanns Eisler was deported. Actor Larry Parks confessed Communist Party membership and was blacklisted anyway. The blacklist demonstrated that fear of being seen to be soft on Communism could make private companies enforce political loyalty more harshly than the state itself.

Even before HUAC’s Hollywood hearings, President Truman’s Executive Order 9835 (March 1947) created the Federal Loyalty Programme. By 1953 around 4.7 million federal employees had been investigated; around 560 had been dismissed and around 6,000 had resigned rather than face investigation. The Internal Security Act of 1950 (the McCarran Act) required Communist organisations to register with the federal government and forbade Communists from working in defence industries. Truman vetoed it; Congress overrode him. State and local loyalty programmes spread further: by 1956 around 13 million Americans had been touched by some kind of loyalty test, often refusing to sign costing public-sector workers their jobs without due process.

Hiss and the Rosenbergs

Two espionage cases convinced wavering Americans that the threat was real. Alger Hiss, a former senior State Department official who had attended the 1945 Yalta Conference with Roosevelt, was accused by ex-Communist Whittaker Chambers in August 1948 of passing documents to the USSR in the 1930s. After two trials Hiss was convicted of perjury in January 1950 and sentenced to five years. The case was prosecuted by a young Republican congressman named Richard Nixon and made his career.

In June 1950 Julius Rosenberg, a New York electrical engineer, was arrested on charges of passing American atomic secrets to the Soviet Union. His wife Ethel was arrested two months later. Both were convicted in March 1951 and executed in the electric chair at Sing Sing in June 1953 — the only Americans executed for espionage in peacetime. Modern declassified Soviet cables (the Venona project) confirm Julius’s espionage; Ethel’s role is more disputed and historians broadly agree she was overcharged. At the time, the case appeared to confirm that Communist subversion reached into American homes.

McCarthy’s Rise, 1950–54

On 9 February 1950 Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin gave a speech at Wheeling, West Virginia. He waved a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known Communists working in the State Department. He never produced the list. The number changed in subsequent speeches (57, then 81). It did not matter. McCarthy’s claim, made at the moment of maximum Cold War anxiety, dominated the news cycle and built him a national following.

Through 1950 to 1954 McCarthy used his Senate Committee on Government Operations to investigate alleged Communists in the State Department, the Voice of America, the Government Printing Office, the Army and even the libraries of US embassies abroad. Witnesses were summoned, careers ended, accusations broadcast. Few Senate colleagues challenged him in public — he had become electorally dangerous. Republican nominee Dwight Eisenhower, campaigning in Wisconsin in October 1952, dropped a planned defence of his friend General George Marshall (whom McCarthy had accused of pro-Communist sympathies) rather than confront McCarthy. The press largely repeated McCarthy’s charges without checking them. Eisenhower privately disliked him but said publicly he ‘would not get in the gutter with that guy’.

The Army-McCarthy Hearings and Decline

McCarthy’s overreach was the Army. In 1954 he turned his accusations on the US Army for protecting an alleged Communist dentist. The Senate televised the hearings between April and June 1954. For 36 days, an audience of around 20 million Americans watched McCarthy bully witnesses, contradict himself and lose his temper. The decisive moment came on 9 June 1954, when Army counsel Joseph Welch confronted him with the now-famous question: ‘Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last?’. Public approval of McCarthy collapsed from around 50% in January 1954 to around 35% by June.

In December 1954 the Senate voted 67–22 to formally censure McCarthy for ‘conduct unbecoming’. He remained a senator but his power was broken. He drank heavily and died of liver failure in May 1957 aged 48. His name became a byword for unsubstantiated political smear — ‘McCarthyism’. The Hollywood blacklist persisted into the 1960s, lifted gradually as Dalton Trumbo and others wrote under their own names again. Federal loyalty programmes were scaled back but not abolished.

The cost of the second Red Scare went well beyond the 320 entertainment-industry blacklisted figures. Universities sacked Marxist academics. Public libraries removed books. Trade unions purged left-wing officers. The State Department lost a generation of China experts who had warned that Chiang Kai-Shek would lose the Chinese civil war — their absence shaped American policy in Asia for years. Civil-rights and women’s organisations were intimidated; the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) felt obliged to expel members it suspected of Communist links. Political dissent in general was narrowed. The phrase ‘guilt by association’ entered everyday speech. Recovery from McCarthyism would take much of the 1960s.

Key Fact

The 1954 televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed McCarthy to around 20 million viewers as a bully and a liar. His approval fell from about 50% (January 1954) to 35% (June 1954). The Senate censured him 67–22 in December 1954. McCarthy died in 1957.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1953 conservative magazine article praising McCarthy for exposing real Communist subversion) and Interpretation B (a 1955 study by a civil-liberties lawyer condemning McCarthyism for destroying careers without evidence). What is the main difference between these views about McCarthyism?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents McCarthy as a defender of national security who uncovered real Communist activity inside the federal government.
• Interpretation B presents McCarthyism as a wave of unsubstantiated smears that destroyed innocent careers and narrowed American freedom of speech.
• Main difference: A frames McCarthy’s investigations as necessary national security work; B frames them as a civil-liberties disaster regardless of any genuine espionage.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1953 conservative magazine article praising McCarthy) and Interpretation B (a 1955 civil-liberties study condemning him) give different views about McCarthyism.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the magazine aimed to support the Republican Party at the height of the Cold War; the study aimed to defend civil liberties against future political smears.
• They use different evidence — the magazine cites the Hiss conviction and the Rosenbergs; the study cites the Hollywood blacklist and innocents fired without due process.
• They were written at different points — the 1953 article was published before the Army-McCarthy hearings exposed McCarthy’s methods; the 1955 study was written after his Senate censure made his methods publicly toxic.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Senator Joseph McCarthy alone caused the climate of fear in 1950s America.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the Red Scare in the United States?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because McCarthy’s February 1950 Wheeling speech, his Senate committee from 1953 and his Army-McCarthy hearings (1954) defined the public face of the Red Scare and gave it his name.
• Convincing because his unsubstantiated accusations made it electorally dangerous for senators, journalists and presidents (including Eisenhower) to challenge him.
• Less convincing because the climate of fear pre-dated McCarthy — HUAC began Hollywood hearings in October 1947, Truman’s federal loyalty programme began in March 1947, and the Hollywood blacklist was in place by November 1947.
• Less convincing because real Cold War events — the Soviet bomb (1949), the Communist victory in China (1949) and the Korean War (1950) — created the anxiety McCarthy exploited; the Hiss conviction (January 1950) and Rosenberg arrest (June 1950) appeared to confirm subversion regardless of McCarthy’s claims.
• Less convincing because by 1953 around 4.7 million federal workers had been investigated under Truman’s order, before McCarthy’s power was at its peak.
• Overall judgement: substantially overstated — McCarthy was a national symbol but the machinery of fear was wider, older and more institutional than one senator.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of HUAC’s 1947 hearings on Hollywood.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Created the Hollywood Ten case — ten writers and directors refused to answer the question on Communist Party membership and were jailed for contempt of Congress between 1947 and 1948.
• Triggered the Hollywood blacklist — the Waldorf Statement (November 1947) announced studios would not employ Communists; around 320 entertainment workers eventually lost their jobs.
• Drove leading figures abroad or into silence — Charlie Chaplin lost his US re-entry permit in 1952; composer Hanns Eisler was deported; many writers worked anonymously under pseudonyms for years.
• Reshaped American film — studios avoided controversial themes about race, poverty or trade unions for years; political conformity in mass culture became the norm and persisted into the early 1960s.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why McCarthyism became such a powerful political force in the United States between 1950 and 1954.
You may consider:
• Cold War setbacks abroad and espionage cases at home
• HUAC, federal loyalty programmes and Senator McCarthy himself.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• External shocks: Soviet atomic bomb (August 1949); Communist victory in China (October 1949); Korean War from June 1950.
• Espionage cases: Alger Hiss convicted of perjury (January 1950); Julius and Ethel Rosenberg arrested (June 1950), convicted (1951) and executed (1953).
• HUAC: October 1947 Hollywood hearings; Hollywood Ten jailed; Waldorf Statement; blacklist of around 320 entertainment workers.
• Truman’s Federal Loyalty Programme (Executive Order 9835, March 1947): around 4.7 million federal workers investigated by 1953; around 560 dismissed.
• McCarran Act 1950: required Communist organisations to register; vetoed by Truman, override by Congress.
• McCarthy’s rise: 9 February 1950 Wheeling speech; chairmanship of Senate Committee on Government Operations 1953–54; investigations of State Department, Voice of America, US Army.
• Press amplification: McCarthy’s charges repeated without checking; few senators willing to confront him.
• Limits: Army-McCarthy hearings (April–June 1954) and Welch’s ‘sense of decency’ rebuke; approval fell from 50% to 35%; Senate censure 67–22 in December 1954.
• Conclusion: McCarthyism was powerful because real Cold War events made fear plausible, federal and corporate machinery turned that fear into action, and McCarthy supplied a name and face to the campaign — but his exposure on television proved that the same media power could break him as quickly as it had built him.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

lessons.title: Civil Rights: Segregation, Martin Luther King and the 1964 Act

before.content_html:
A Country Two Americas

In 1954, around 90 years after the abolition of slavery, around 17 million African-Americans lived under Jim Crow — a system of state and local laws that segregated schools, drinking fountains, hospitals, swimming pools, restaurants, lavatories, buses and railway carriages. In southern states, fewer than 5% of eligible black voters were registered. Lynching had killed thousands of black Americans since Reconstruction. The Supreme Court’s 1896 decision in Plessy v Ferguson had given the system legal cover under the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’. Civil-rights victories between 1954 and 1968 were not the work of one leader, one bus boycott or one act of Congress. They required mass struggle — and the willingness of ordinary black Americans to face arrest, beating and worse.

Key Fact

Under Jim Crow, schools, buses, restaurants and drinking fountains were segregated across southern states. Fewer than 5% of eligible black voters were registered in the South in 1954. Civil-rights victories between 1954 and 1968 came from mass action, not just key leaders.

Brown v Board and Little Rock

The first decisive break came on 17 May 1954. In Brown v Board of Education the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that segregated schools were unconstitutional, overturning Plessy v Ferguson. NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall argued the case using research showing that segregation harmed black children psychologically. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that ‘separate educational facilities are inherently unequal’.

Implementation was another matter. Southern states pursued ‘massive resistance’. In September 1957 nine African-American students attempted to enrol at Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas. Governor Orval Faubus ordered the Arkansas National Guard to block them. Faced with images of bayonet-wielding soldiers turning back schoolchildren, President Eisenhower — reluctant to act — sent in 1,000 paratroopers from the 101st Airborne to escort the ‘Little Rock Nine’ into school for the year. Federal supremacy was established but in southern schools desegregation crawled: by 1964, only around 2% of southern black students were in formerly all-white schools.

Montgomery and the Rise of King

On 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks — a 42-year-old NAACP secretary in Montgomery, Alabama — refused to give up her seat on a city bus to a white passenger. She was arrested. The local NAACP and a young Baptist minister named Martin Luther King launched the Montgomery Bus Boycott. For 381 days, around 40,000 black residents of Montgomery walked, carpooled or rode mule-drawn carts rather than ride the buses. The boycott bankrupted the bus company. In November 1956 the Supreme Court ruled segregation on city buses unconstitutional.

King became the national face of peaceful protest. Drawing on Gandhi’s teaching and Christian theology, he founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) in 1957. Sit-ins began at a Greensboro, North Carolina, lunch counter in February 1960 and spread to 54 cities; around 70,000 students — black and white — took part. The Freedom Rides of May 1961 sent integrated busloads of activists into the Deep South to test the desegregation of inter-state bus terminals. They were attacked by white mobs in Anniston and Birmingham; the Kennedy administration eventually sent federal marshals to protect them.

In April 1963, King launched a campaign in Birmingham, Alabama — one of the most segregated cities in America. Police commissioner ‘Bull’ Connor used dogs and high-pressure fire hoses against teenage protestors in May. Television images of children being knocked off their feet by water cannon shocked the nation. King was arrested and wrote his ‘Letter from Birmingham Jail’ defending non-violent direct action. On 28 August 1963, around 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom; King delivered the ‘I have a dream’ speech. In March 1965 marchers at Selma, Alabama, were attacked by state troopers on Edmund Pettus Bridge in scenes broadcast on national television (‘Bloody Sunday’). The combination of mass non-violent protest and state-sponsored violence pushed Congress and President Johnson into action.

Malcolm X and the Black Power Movement

Not all African-Americans accepted King’s commitment to non-violence and integration. Malcolm Little, born 1925, became Malcolm X after joining the Nation of Islam in prison. As the Nation’s most powerful speaker through the 1950s and early 1960s, he attacked white supremacy directly, advocated black self-defence (‘by any means necessary’), and rejected integration with what he called ‘a burning house’. He left the Nation in 1964 after a falling-out with Elijah Muhammad, made the pilgrimage to Mecca and began moving towards a more orthodox Islam and a position closer to mainstream civil rights. He was assassinated in February 1965 by Nation of Islam gunmen.

After 1965, with the major civil-rights laws passed but urban black poverty unchanged, the Black Power Movement grew. Stokely Carmichael coined the slogan in 1966; the Black Panther Party, founded by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland, California, in October 1966, ran community programmes (free breakfasts for around 20,000 children) alongside armed patrols of police in black neighbourhoods. At the 1968 Mexico Olympics, sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists during the medal ceremony. Riots tore through Watts (Los Angeles, 1965, 34 dead), Newark and Detroit (1967, 43 dead in Detroit) and 100 American cities after King’s assassination in April 1968.

The Civil Rights Acts of 1964 and 1968

The legislative breakthroughs came under President Johnson. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 (signed 2 July) banned segregation in public places (hotels, restaurants, swimming pools, theatres) and discrimination in employment. The Voting Rights Act of August 1965 outlawed the literacy tests and intimidation that had kept southern black voters off electoral rolls; black voter registration in Mississippi rose from around 7% in 1964 to around 67% by 1969. The Civil Rights Act of 1968 (the Fair Housing Act, signed days after King’s death) banned racial discrimination in renting and selling housing — tackling the redlining that had locked black families out of suburbs. Together the three acts dismantled the legal structure of Jim Crow.

Implementation remained slow. Schools, despite Brown, remained largely segregated by neighbourhood. Police violence and economic inequality continued. By the early 1970s the formal civil-rights movement had won its central legal battles but new questions — affirmative action, busing, urban poverty — had taken its place.

Examiner reports flag a recurring student weakness: collapsing civil rights into ‘Martin Luther King had a dream and signed the Civil Rights Act’. The legal victories required ordinary people to risk their lives. Around 40,000 walked in Montgomery for 381 days. Around 70,000 took part in the sit-ins. Tens of thousands of black voters in Mississippi faced beating and arrest to register. The leaders — King, Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Stokely Carmichael — mattered but only because mass action made their leadership consequential. The 1964 Civil Rights Act would not have been signed without Birmingham’s televised police violence; the 1965 Voting Rights Act would not have passed without Selma. Federal action followed mass struggle, not the other way around.

Key Fact

The 1964 Civil Rights Act banned segregation in public places and employment discrimination, after Birmingham. The 1965 Voting Rights Act outlawed literacy tests, after Selma. The 1968 Fair Housing Act banned housing discrimination, after King’s assassination.
before.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Evaluate questions on King vs Malcolm X, the strongest answers handle them as connected strands of one struggle, not opposites — King provided respectability and federal pressure; Malcolm X gave political space to Black Power and attacked white liberal complacency. For 12-mark Period Essays comparing the importance of leaders against mass struggle, the misconception to avoid is ‘civil rights = MLK’. Examiner reports stress that ordinary participants in Montgomery, Birmingham, Selma and Mississippi voter-registration drives mattered as much as the leaders.

lessons.title: The Great Society, Feminism and Roe v Wade

before.content_html:
Two Reformist Presidencies

When John F. Kennedy was sworn in on 20 January 1961, he was 43 years old, the first Catholic president, and his inaugural address asked Americans ‘ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country’. His domestic agenda — the New Frontier — promised federal aid to education, healthcare for the elderly and a higher minimum wage. Most of these bills stalled in a Congress dominated by southern Democrats. Kennedy’s legislative record was thin. After his assassination on 22 November 1963, his vice-president Lyndon Johnson used Kennedy’s memory to push through the most ambitious domestic reform programme since the New Deal — the Great Society.

Key Fact

Kennedy’s New Frontier produced the Equal Pay Act 1963 but most legislation stalled. Johnson’s Great Society from 1964 delivered the Civil Rights Act, Medicare and Medicaid, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and the War on Poverty — the most ambitious reform programme since the New Deal.

Johnson’s Great Society

Johnson, a Texas Democrat and former Senate majority leader, declared an ‘unconditional war on poverty’ in his January 1964 State of the Union address. The 1964 Economic Opportunity Act created Job Corps (vocational training for poor young people), Head Start (pre-school for poor children, eventually serving around 700,000 children a year), and Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA, a domestic Peace Corps). Around 22% of Americans had lived in poverty in 1959; by 1973 the figure had fallen to around 11%, the largest reduction in American history.

Healthcare was transformed. The 1965 Medicare programme provided federal health insurance for Americans aged over 65; Medicaid in the same year provided healthcare for the very poor. The two programmes covered around 19 million elderly and 10 million low-income Americans by 1969 — healthcare access on a scale the New Deal had been unable to deliver. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act of April 1965 sent over $1 billion of federal money to schools serving poor children, the first major federal aid to education in American history. The Immigration and Nationality Act of October 1965 abolished the 1924 quota system that had favoured northern Europeans, opening the door to immigration from Asia, Africa and Latin America.

The Great Society was undermined by Johnson’s own Vietnam War. American military spending in Vietnam rose from around $100 million a year in 1964 to roughly $20 billion a year by 1968 — money that could not also fund anti-poverty programmes. By 1968 around half a million American troops were in Vietnam and around 16,500 had been killed. Public opinion turned, especially among young Americans facing the draft. Johnson announced in March 1968 that he would not seek re-election. Richard Nixon won the November 1968 election promising ‘peace with honour’. The reform energy of the Great Society did not survive Vietnam.

The Feminine Mystique and the New Women’s Movement

In 1963, Smith College graduate Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique — a book based on a survey of her former classmates that asked ‘is this all there is?’. Friedan argued the post-war ideal of suburban housewifery left educated women trapped, depressed and unfulfilled — what she called ‘the problem that has no name’. The book sold around 3 million copies in three years and gave a vocabulary to a generation of women who had absorbed the post-war domestic ideal and found it hollow.

In June 1966 Friedan and twenty-seven other women, including Pauli Murray and Aileen Hernandez, founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) — sometimes called ‘the NAACP for women’. NOW lobbied for equal pay, anti-discrimination enforcement, federal childcare and reproductive rights. Membership grew from 300 in 1966 to around 40,000 by 1974. NOW was a moderate, integrationist organisation; younger women’s liberation groups (Redstockings, the Furies) pushed harder on cultural and personal politics.

Equal Pay, Title VII and the 1972 Equal Rights Ruling

The Equal Pay Act of June 1963, signed by Kennedy, made it illegal to pay men and women different wages for equivalent work. Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex (the word ‘sex’ was added by a southern segregationist congressman, Howard W. Smith, who hoped to defeat the bill; it passed anyway). In 1972 the Educational Amendments included Title IX, banning sex discrimination in any federally funded education programme — transformative for women’s sport, science and graduate study. The Supreme Court’s 1972 ruling in Reed v Reed extended equal-protection guarantees to women on the same basis as race — a major constitutional shift. Women’s share of the federal civil service workforce, share of medical and law school admissions, and visibility in the workplace all rose sharply through the 1970s.

Roe v Wade and the Limits of Reform

On 22 January 1973 the Supreme Court ruled by 7–2 in Roe v Wade that state laws banning abortion violated a constitutional right to privacy. ‘Jane Roe’ was the legal pseudonym of Norma McCorvey, a Dallas waitress who had been unable to obtain a legal abortion under Texas law. The decision legalised abortion across the United States. It was hailed by NOW and women’s liberation groups as a decisive victory for reproductive rights.

It also produced the most durable opposition. The proposed Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), passed by Congress in March 1972, would have written sex equality into the Constitution. It needed ratification by 38 states. By the original 1979 deadline only 35 states had ratified. The defeat was largely the work of one woman: Phyllis Schlafly, a Catholic conservative whose STOP ERA campaign argued that the amendment would force women into the military draft, end alimony, abolish single-sex bathrooms and undermine the family. Schlafly mobilised middle-class housewives across the South and Midwest. The ERA expired unratified in 1982. Roe v Wade itself was overturned by the Supreme Court in 2022.

Schlafly’s STOP ERA campaign was effective for several reasons. Many married women in the early 1970s benefited from a legal regime that gave them alimony, presumed custody and exemption from the draft, and feared losing those protections. The campaign reframed feminism as a threat to family security rather than an expansion of women’s opportunity. The amendment’s wording was vague enough to allow opponents to argue it would have unforeseen consequences (gay marriage, mixed-sex bathrooms, women in combat). Reformers also misread the politics: by 1977 the women’s movement had grown more radical and lost some moderate support; Roe v Wade made abortion central to the debate, alienating many religious women. By 1973 American feminism had won landmark victories (Equal Pay Act, Title VII, Title IX, Roe) but the conservative backlash had organised. The 1980 Reagan election would mark its political arrival.

Key Fact

The Equal Pay Act 1963 banned wage discrimination by sex; Title IX 1972 banned sex discrimination in federally funded education; the ERA would have written sex equality into the Constitution but failed ratification by 1982. Roe v Wade 1973 legalised abortion across the United States.
before.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Evaluate questions on the Great Society, examiner reports flag students who treat Vietnam as separate from the reform programme. The strongest answers track how Vietnam costs (around $20 billion a year by 1968) and political toxicity drained resources and energy from anti-poverty work. For 12-mark Period Essays on the women’s movement, the misconception is ‘feminism = NOW’. Cover NOW, the radical women’s liberation groups, the legal cases (Reed v Reed, Roe v Wade) and the ERA defeat as connected strands of one debate that produced both major gains and a powerful conservative backlash.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kennedy’s New Frontier mostly stalled in Congress; Johnson’s Great Society from 1964 delivered Medicare, Medicaid, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, the War on Poverty and the 1965 Immigration Act — the largest reform programme since the New Deal.
  • Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963) and the founding of NOW (1966) launched the new women’s movement; the Equal Pay Act 1963, Title VII 1964, Title IX 1972 and Reed v Reed 1972 transformed the legal status of women.
  • Roe v Wade (January 1973) legalised abortion; Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA campaign defeated the proposed Equal Rights Amendment by 1982 and signalled the conservative backlash that ended the reform era.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1972 NOW campaign leaflet calling the Equal Rights Amendment essential to ending sex discrimination) and Interpretation B (a 1973 STOP ERA pamphlet by Phyllis Schlafly arguing the amendment would harm American families). What is the main difference between these views about the women’s movement?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the ERA as the constitutional foundation of equal pay, equal employment and the next stage of women’s legal rights.
• Interpretation B presents the ERA as a threat to family security, alimony, single-sex bathrooms and the existing legal protections that benefited married women.
• Main difference: A frames the women’s movement as the completion of unfinished civil-rights work; B frames it as an attack on the family that ordinary women would lose by.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1972 NOW campaign leaflet) and Interpretation B (a 1973 STOP ERA pamphlet by Phyllis Schlafly) give different views about the women’s movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the NOW leaflet aimed to mobilise career women and progressive activists; Schlafly’s pamphlet aimed to mobilise religious housewives in the South and Midwest.
• They use different evidence — NOW cited employment-discrimination cases and the Equal Pay Act; Schlafly cited the threat of military conscription, ending alimony and mixed-sex facilities.
• They were produced from different ideological positions — a feminist organisation pushing constitutional amendment versus a Catholic conservative defending traditional family roles.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society was the most successful reform programme since the New Deal.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about Johnson’s domestic reforms?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the 1964 Civil Rights Act, the 1965 Voting Rights Act and the 1968 Fair Housing Act ended legal segregation and dramatically increased black voter registration.
• Convincing because Medicare and Medicaid (1965) gave around 19 million elderly and 10 million poor Americans federal health insurance, an achievement the New Deal had not managed.
• Convincing because the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965) was the first major federal aid to education in American history, sending over $1 billion to schools serving poor children.
• Convincing because the poverty rate fell from around 22% in 1959 to around 11% by 1973 — the largest reduction in American history.
• Less convincing because Vietnam War spending rose to around $20 billion a year by 1968 and undermined the War on Poverty financially and politically.
• Less convincing because urban riots in Watts (1965), Detroit (1967) and after King’s death (1968) showed that the underlying inequalities the Great Society addressed were not solved.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on legislative breadth and impact — comparable to the New Deal in scope and arguably greater in lasting reach — but undercut politically by Vietnam.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963) on American women.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gave a vocabulary to widespread female dissatisfaction with the post-war suburban ideal — ‘the problem that has no name’ named the gap between expectation and lived experience for educated white women.
• Sold around 3 million copies in three years, reaching a mass middle-class audience and prompting consciousness-raising groups across the country.
• Helped inspire the founding of the National Organization for Women in June 1966, with Friedan as its first president; NOW grew from 300 to around 40,000 members by 1974.
• Reframed feminism as a programme for educated women in employment as well as a civil-rights project — setting the agenda for Title VII enforcement, Title IX (1972) and the push for the Equal Rights Amendment.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the women’s movement won major legal victories between 1963 and 1973.
You may consider:
• new women’s organisations and writers, such as Friedan and NOW
• reform-minded presidents and Congresses.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963): around 3 million copies sold; named ‘the problem that has no name’.
• Equal Pay Act (June 1963), signed by Kennedy: banned wage discrimination on grounds of sex.
• Title VII of Civil Rights Act (1964): banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex; word ‘sex’ added by Howard W. Smith.
• Founding of NOW (June 1966): Friedan, Pauli Murray, Aileen Hernandez and 24 others; lobbied for equal pay, anti-discrimination enforcement, childcare and reproductive rights.
• Younger women’s liberation groups (Redstockings, the Furies) pushed harder on cultural and personal politics.
• Title IX (1972): banned sex discrimination in any federally funded education programme; transformative for women’s sport, science and graduate study.
• Reed v Reed (1972): Supreme Court extended equal-protection guarantees to women.
• Roe v Wade (January 1973): legalised abortion across the United States.
• Reform-minded presidents: Kennedy (Equal Pay Act), Johnson (Title VII), Nixon (signed Title IX).
• Conclusion: the legal victories combined writers and organisations naming the problem (Friedan, NOW), allies in the federal government during a reform decade, and Supreme Court rulings extending civil-rights logic from race to sex. The defeat of the ERA and the lasting controversy over Roe show the limits of the same period.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Great Society programme launched by Lyndon Johnson from 1964.

• It established Medicare in 1965 to provide federal health insurance for Americans over 65 and Medicaid in 1965 for the very poor; together the programmes covered around 29 million Americans by 1969.
• The Elementary and Secondary Education Act (April 1965) was the first major federal aid to education, sending over $1 billion to schools serving poor children.
• The 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act abolished the 1924 quota system that had favoured northern Europeans, opening the door to immigration from Asia, Africa and Latin America.
